parts.text: Give two diagnostic tests to diagnose osteomyelitis.
In the emergency department she was started on cephalexin. The lesion is worsening with necrotic skin at the edges. What are two things to do to manage this patient?

parts_raw.text: 2 diagnostic tests to diagnose osteomyelitis.
In the emerg, she was started on cephalexin. The lesion is worsening with necrotic skin at the edges of the lesion. What are 2 things to do to manage this patient?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Probe-to-bone test of the ulcer (a chronic ulcer >2 cm2 or positive probe-to-bone has high positive predictive value; specificity 91%). (2) MRI of the foot (pooled sensitivity 90%, specificity 79%); definitive diagnosis is by percutaneous/transcutaneous bone biopsy for culture and histology.
b) (1) Urgent surgical consultation for débridement/drainage of infected and necrotic bone and soft tissue, with deep operative bone and soft-tissue specimens sent for aerobic and anaerobic culture. (2) Stop cephalexin and start broad-spectrum parenteral therapy covering the polymicrobial aerobic and anaerobic flora (e.g. piperacillin-tazobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam or ertapenem, or a beta-lactam plus metronidazole), plus vascular assessment for revascularization; antimicrobials should not be withheld for cultures given local signs of spreading infection.

cohort_answer.text: X-ray, MRI/bone scan, probe to bone. || Surgical/orthopaedic consult for debridement of wound/necrotic areas + send for culture; Initiate IV antibiotics.

questions.question: A 21-month-old child has discitis.
questions.question_raw: PM 25. Discitis in 21 month old - What are the 2 most likely pathogens to cover with empiric therapy? (1) Why do children over the age of 7 rarely get discitis? (1)

parts.text: Name the two most likely pathogens to cover with empiric therapy.

parts_raw.text: 2 most likely pathogens to cover with empiric therapy
Why do children over the age of 7 rarely get discitis?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus. (2) Kingella kingae (the dominant pathogen of osteoarticular infection in children under 4 years).
b) Discitis in young children arises from hematogenous seeding of the intervertebral disk through vascular channels that cross the vertebral end plate and penetrate the anulus/nucleus. These intraosseous vascular channels involute and are essentially gone by about age 7-8, so the disk becomes avascular and can no longer be seeded hematogenously; older children and adults instead develop vertebral osteomyelitis with secondary disk involvement.
questions.beyond_mandell: Mandell states K. kingae and S. aureus are the leading prepubertal hematogenous osteoarticular pathogens and that the disk is seeded hematogenously, but the age-related regression of disk vascular supply comes from pediatric literature (CPS osteoarticular infection statement 2018).

questions.question: Explain why children older than 7 years rarely develop discitis.

parts.text: Why children older than 7 years do not get discitis very often.

parts_raw.text: Why children older than 7 don't get discitis very often

questions.model_answer: Discitis results from hematogenous seeding of the intervertebral disk. In young children the disk retains vascular channels crossing the cartilaginous end plate; these vessels progressively involute and disappear by roughly 7-8 years of age, leaving the disk avascular. Without a blood supply the disk can no longer be seeded during transient bacteraemia, so beyond that age infection presents as vertebral osteomyelitis with contiguous end plate/disk spread rather than primary discitis.
questions.beyond_mandell: Age-related regression of intervertebral disk vascularity is from pediatric literature (CPS osteoarticular infection statement 2018); Mandell states only that the disk space is seeded hematogenously.

cohort_answer.text: Less vascularized when older than 7 and infection is hematogenously spread

What 4 bacterial groups / types (use specific pathogen names if relevant or pathogen group if not) guide empiric therapy?

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Strict glycemic control and smoking cessation, with foot care/well-cushioned pressure-redistributing footwear and offloading. (2) Assessment of arterial supply (pedal pulses, Doppler/ankle-brachial index, transcutaneous oxygen pressure) with revascularization if perfusion is poor. (3) Surgical débridement of infected and necrotic bone and soft tissue with dead-space management, obtaining deep intraoperative cultures before antimicrobials where safe to wait. (4) Evaluation for contiguous osteomyelitis (probe-to-bone, imaging, bone biopsy) and treatment with an appropriate-duration antimicrobial course guided by those cultures.
b) Probe-to-bone and inspection of the ulcer (chronic ulcer >2 cm2 or positive probe-to-bone has high positive predictive value; sensitivity 60%, specificity 91%); plain radiograph; MRI (sensitivity 90%, specificity 79%); vascular assessment with ankle-brachial index/Doppler; transcutaneous bone biopsy or deep operative bone culture for aerobic and anaerobic culture and histology, which is the diagnostic standard.
c) (1) Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA). (2) Streptococci, including group B Streptococcus. (3) Aerobic gram-negative bacilli (Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa). (4) Anaerobes. These infections are usually polymicrobial, hence broad-spectrum regimens such as piperacillin-tazobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam, ertapenem, or a beta-lactam plus metronidazole.

cohort_answer.text:
Management: glycemic control, wound care, offloading, vascular assessment --- consult vascular/ortho, evaluation for osteomyelitis, deep tissue cultures – bx or curettage of infected tissue cultures.
Empiric therapy coverage: Pseudomonas, anaerobes, Staphylococcus aureus, Streptococcus sp, aerobic GNB, Enterococcus

questions.model_answer:
a) Radiographs are insensitive early; bony abnormalities appear about 10 to 14 days (CPS: 7-21 days) after onset of infection.
b) (1) Localized periosteal elevation/periosteal new bone formation. (2) Metaphyseal lytic (lucent) destructive lesions.
c) Staphylococcus aureus, methicillin susceptible in most Canadian children (Kingella kingae is the other main pathogen under age 4). Treat with cefazolin (or nafcillin/oxacillin) intravenously, stepping down to oral cephalexin once afebrile and clinically improved; cefazolin also covers K. kingae. Add vancomycin empirically only where MRSA prevalence is high.
d) Minimum 3 weeks of total therapy (Mandell: typical pediatric duration 3 weeks), commonly extended to 3-4 weeks depending on clinical and CRP response.
questions.beyond_mandell: CPS 2018 osteoarticular infection statement: 7-21 day radiographic window, cefazolin then oral cephalexin, and step-down when afebrile with >50% CRP fall.

cohort_answer.text: X-ray changes seen 7-21 days after onset of symptoms: Lytic lesions and localized periosteal lifting. 'Current data support both the probability that K kingae is the dominant pathogen in children younger than 4 years old presenting with SA (with or without OA) and that S aureus is the more common pathogen in older children' (CPS statement osteoarticular infections). Treatment: Cefazolin followed by cephalexin oral stepdown when clinically improved, afebrile and CRP reduction 50%. Duration: 3-4 weeks depending on clinical response

questions.model_answer:
a) Radiographs are insensitive early; bony abnormality is usually seen 10 to 14 days after onset (CPS: 7-21 days); soft tissue swelling may appear within the first few days.
b) (1) Periosteal elevation with periosteal new bone formation. (2) Metaphyseal lytic/lucent destructive lesions (sclerosis follows after about a month).
c) Staphylococcus aureus. Treat methicillin-susceptible disease with intravenous cefazolin or nafcillin/oxacillin, stepping down to oral cephalexin once afebrile and improving; use vancomycin if MRSA is suspected or prevalent. Purulent joint involvement also requires surgical drainage/arthrotomy.
d) Minimum 3 weeks of total therapy for uncomplicated disease (Mandell: typical pediatric duration 3 weeks), commonly 3-4 weeks, and longer (4-6 weeks) for complicated infection or hip septic arthritis.
questions.beyond_mandell: CPS 2018 osteoarticular infection statement supplies the 7-21 day radiographic window and the 3-4 week (up to 4-6 week) duration ranges.

cohort_answer.text: X-ray changes: soft tissue swelling at 3 days; lytic lesions, periosteal elevation, periosteal new bone formation at 10-20 days (7-21 days per CPS); sclerosis of bone after a month. Most common changes: periosteal reaction (new bone formation) and periosteal elevation (suggests abscess). Bug/treatment: Staph aureus (MSSA or MRSA depending on local epidemiology), Cloxacillin or Cefazolin for MSSA, Vancomycin for MRSA. Duration: 3-6 weeks (septic arthritis 3 weeks minimum, OM 4-6 weeks); uncomplicated AO/SA generally 3-4 weeks (4-6 weeks for hip SA).

parts.text: Four investigations according to IDSA guidelines
Four specific organisms (or organism groups) that would cause infection in this patient

parts_raw.text: 4 investigations according to IDSA guidelines
4 specific organisms (or organism groups) that would cause infection in this patient

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Careful foot/ulcer examination with a probe-to-bone test (positive probe-to-bone or exposed bone has high positive predictive value for contiguous osteomyelitis; sensitivity 60%, specificity 91%). (2) Plain radiographs of the foot for bone destruction, followed by MRI (pooled sensitivity 90%, specificity 79%) when osteomyelitis, abscess or deep soft-tissue infection is suspected. (3) Deep specimens for culture - transcutaneous/percutaneous bone biopsy or operative deep bone and soft-tissue cultures sent for aerobic and anaerobic culture (and histology); superficial swabs are inadequate, and antimicrobials should be withheld until deep cultures are taken unless there are local or systemic signs requiring immediate therapy. (4) Vascular assessment: palpation of pedal pulses plus noninvasive testing (Doppler/ABI, transcutaneous oxygen pressure, angiography if revascularization is contemplated).
b) (1) Staphylococcus aureus, including MRSA (which causes CA-MRSA bone infection and would not be covered by cephalexin). (2) Streptococci, particularly group B Streptococcus (Streptococcus agalactiae), which is increasingly identified in diabetic bone infection. (3) Aerobic gram-negative bacilli - Enterobacterales and Pseudomonas aeruginosa. (4) Anaerobes (foul/brown discharge; molecular studies show anaerobes are underdetected by conventional culture) - these infections are typically polymicrobial, requiring broad-spectrum therapy such as piperacillin-tazobactam, ampicillin-sulbactam or ertapenem, or a beta-lactam/quinolone plus metronidazole.

cohort_answer.text: Investigations: properly obtained wound cultures, ABI (esp if pedal pulses absent, monofilament 10g nylon test), plain film to rule out OM, MRI if suspecting OM/abscess. Organisms: MRSA, Pseudomonas, GNB including ESBL, Anaerobes, CONS (also Peptoniphilus, Finegoldia, Anaerococcus, Corynebacterium, Staphylococcus per Mandell's)

questions.question: Pediatric spinal infections.

parts.text: Why is discitis not as commonly seen in children older than 7?
What are the two most common organisms to which antibiotic therapy should be tailored?

parts_raw.text: A) Why is discitis not as commonly seen in kids older than 7?
B) What are the 2 most common organisms to which antibiotic tx should be tailored?

questions.model_answer:
a) Because the vascular anatomy of the disc changes with age. In young children the intervertebral disc is richly vascularized by vessels crossing the cartilaginous vertebral end plate into the anulus, so transient bacteremia seeds the disc itself; these intraosseous/transdiscal vessels progressively involute and are obliterated by about 7 to 10 years of age, leaving only a peripheral anastomotic network. After that age hematogenous seeding lodges in the vertebral body metaphyseal equivalent rather than the disc, so infection presents as vertebral osteomyelitis/spondylodiscitis rather than isolated discitis.
b) (1) Staphylococcus aureus (including MRSA, a recognized cause of discitis in children). (2) Kingella kingae, particularly in children under about 4 years.
questions.beyond_mandell: The age-related involution of the vertebral end-plate/disc vessels is pediatric orthopedic-infection teaching (Feigin/Mandell pediatric osteomyelitis literature); Chapter 104 states only that hematogenous disc-space seeding occurs and names S. aureus and K. kingae as leading pediatric pathogens.

cohort_answer.text:
Unlike adults, intervertebral disc in children is richly vascularized (vessels across cartilaginous vertebral plate into ring). After age 8 these vessels disappear but a rich anastomotic network remains peripherally. Rich vasculature <7 years enables bacterial emboli deposition within disc with possible extension to endplates/vertebral bodies
S. aureus; Kingella kingae

questions.model_answer:
a) (1) Staphylococcus aureus. (2) Kingella kingae (typically under 4 years, often under 2); in a very young infant, group B Streptococcus and Escherichia coli - the organisms of neonatal sepsis - are also important considerations.
b) Young children have a richly vascularized intervertebral disc, with vessels crossing the cartilaginous vertebral end plate; hematogenous seeding during bacteremia therefore deposits in the disc first rather than in bone. Kingella kingae colonizes the posterior pharynx of young children and invades during viral respiratory illness. These transdiscal vessels involute by about 7 to 10 years of age, after which discitis becomes rare.
questions.beyond_mandell: Kingella pharyngeal colonization and age-related disc vascular involution come from pediatric osteoarticular infection literature, not Chapter 104.

cohort_answer.text:
S. aureus; Kingella kingae (less than 4 years, usually under 2)
Children more commonly colonized with Kingella in posterior pharynx - can lead to discitis/OM especially during respiratory infections. Intervertebral discs highly vascularized in children, easily hematogenously seeded. Blood vessels present in cartilaginous vertebral endplate until ~7 years, causing disc infection first rather than bone; after 10 years vessels obliterated
